Creating Climate-Resilient Communities through Vacant Lot Restoration

National Wildlife, 06 29, 2021

Video (5:36)
Description

Over the last two years, National Wildlife Federation piloted a project with the Pennsylvania Horticultural Society’s Philadelphia LandCare program to transform a network of vacant lots into climate-resilient wildlife habitat. We wanted to explore how cities with vacant lots can restore these sites to provide pollinator habitat, green stormwater infrastructure, equitable access to nearby nature, and create economic/job training opportunities.

Learn more: 1) https://www.nwf.org/Magazines/National-Wildlife/2021/April-May/Conservation/Lot-Revival 2) https://blog.nwf.org/2021/02/vacant-lots-to-pollinator-habitat-in-philadelphia-pa/

Transcript
Transforming communities

0:00 · I mean, for me, it’s inspirational and it gives me hope in seeing investment from the city, from nonprofits, from community members transforming lots that are public health hazards and eyesores, and dangerous, and turning them into usable, safe, beautiful green spaces.

0:25 · Yeah, I love it.

0:27 · It It’s making a difference. It’s making an impact in people’s lives.

The land care program

0:34 · The city of Philadelphia is a post-industrial city, and so we have a lot of vacant lots in the city. And unfortunately, most of them, whether they’re privately owned or city-owned, don’t have the capacity to maintain them.

0:47 · And so they grow heavy weeds, and, you know, people dump their trash on there, and there’s debris, and it’s just It’s an eyesore. It’s not something that people deserve to live by.

0:58 · So that’s where we at PHS come in. We have our Philadelphia Land Care program, where we completely clean and green these vacant lots, so that you know, what was formerly a terrible eyesore is now a community asset, which people can use, and people can enjoy, and they feel safer around.

1:17 · Through this project, we’re trying to change the narrative behind vacant lots, and switching it from a detriment and a negative to a community asset, and realizing that we have all this open, accessible land, and that it could serve as easy and equitable access to nature and to green space in urban environments, but it can also provide ecological habitat as well.

Greening and infrastructure

1:42 · We’ve noticed the soil quality has improved, which helps with drainage. And we In Philadelphia, have a lot of of stormwater management issues when it rains heavily.

Extreme Heat Is the New Normal

New York Times Opinion, 08 28, 2026

Video (15:42)
Description

We filmed “A New Inferno,” the short documentary above, in Phoenix, one of the hottest cities in America, through some of the city’s hottest days of 2025, during one of the hottest years on record globally. On one of our production days, temperatures reached 118 while we were filming outside.

In the face of extreme heat, we documented firefighters and paramedics of the Phoenix Fire Department saving lives in real time. We wanted to call attention to a specialized technique of ice bag immersion for people facing life-threatening heat stroke. We hope that telling their story and showcasing the efficacy of this strategy will encourage wider adoption of this protocol across the country.

Yet this procedure is ultimately a stopgap, as firefighters do their best to adapt to the climate crisis in front of them. The underlying story of heat in Phoenix is one of broader, interlocking crises: homelessness and substance use disorders that are deeply entangled with urban heat, each amplifying the other, illustrating how climate change affects the disenfranchised most brutally.

With our film, we aim to reframe how the public thinks about heat: as an invisible, silent killer reshaping the rhythms of urban life.

Documentary and text by By Nita Blum-Reddick and Jonathan Pickett

In 1968, Congress passed the Fair Housing Act that made it illegal to discriminate in housing. Gene Demby of NPR’s Code Switch explains why neighborhoods are still so segregated today.

It’s the fearless conversations about race that you’ve been waiting for! Hosted by journalists of color, our podcast tackles the subject of race head-on. 0:22 · And he’s not wrong, because if you look at the way housing segregation works in America you can see how things ended up this way.

0:28 · Once you see it, you won’t be able to unsee it.

0:31 · OK, let’s look at MLK Boulevard in Baltimore.

0:35 · I want to show you how to see housing segregation in schools, in health, in family wealth, in policing.

0:41 · But first, an explanatory comma.

0:45 · It’s the 1930s in the wake of the Great Depression.

0:47 · FDR is president.

0:48 · He wants to bring economic relief to millions of Americans through a collection of federal programs and projects called The New Deal.

0:54 · One part of that “new deal” was The National Housing Act of 1934, which introduced ideas like the 30-year mortgage and low, fixed interest rates.

1:03 · So now you have all these lower-income people who can afford homes, but how do you make sure they don’t default on their new mortgages?

1:09 · Enter the Home Owners Loan Corp.

1:12 · The HOLC created residential security maps.

RESIDENTIAL SECURITY MAPS

1:15 · And these maps? They’re where the term redlining comes from.

1:20 · Green meant “best area, best people,” aka businessmen; blue meant “good people,” like white-collar families; yellow meant a “declining area,” with working class families; and red meant “detrimental influences, hazardous,” like “foreign-born” people, “low-class whites,” and – most significantly – “Negroes.”

1:41 · Again and again on these HOLC maps, one of the most consistent criteria for redlined neighborhoods is the presence of black and

brown people.

1:49 · Let’s be clear.

1:50 · Studies show that people who lived in redlined areas were not necessarily more likely to default on their mortgages.

1:57 · But redlining made it difficult — if not impossible — to buy or refinance.

2:02 · So landlords abandon their properties.

2:04 · City services become unreliable.

2:06 · In most places, crime increases.

2:09 · And property values drop.

2:11 · All of these conditions fester for 30 years as white people flee to the brand new suburbs popping up all over the country.

2:18 · Many of those suburbs institute rules, called covenants, that explicitly forbid selling homes to black people.

2:23 · And all of this was perfectly legal.

2:27 · Now it’s 1968.

2:29 · And MLK is assassinated.

2:31 · News Report: Good evening.

2:32 · The Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King, 39 years old, The apostle of nonviolence in the civil rights movement has been shot to death in Memphis, Tenn.

2:39 · Martin Luther King was shot and was killed tonight in Memphis, Tenn.

2:42 · In the aftermath, Congress passes the Fair Housing Act of 1968.

2:47 · It’s a policy meant to encourage equal housing opportunities regardless of race, or religion or national origin.

2:52 · And it offers protections for future homeowners and renters, but does little to fix the damage already done.

2:58 · Over the next 50 years, the Fair Housing Act is rarely enforced.

3:02 · So you can still see housing segregation and its effects, in Baltimore and often along any MLK Boulevard in any U.S. city.

3:11 · Like its effects on wealth.

WEALTH

3:13 · So homeownership is the major way Americans create wealth, right?

3:16 · Well, discrimination in housing is the major reason that black families up and down the income scale have a tiny fraction of the family wealth that white families do – even white families with less education and lower incomes.

3:28 · For almost 30 years, 98 percent of FHA loans were handed out to white borrowers.

3:33 · Not only were black neighborhoods redlined, and not only was the Fair Housing Act selectively enforced, if at all, but it is still today much harder for a black person to get a mortgage or home loan than it is for a white person.

3:46 · John: Families are fearful of speaking up about a basic human right that should be afforded to everyone in the world but definitely in the richest country in the world.

3:59 · And housing segregation in schools.

4:02 · The primary way that Americans pay for public schools is by paying property taxes.

4:07 · People who live in more valuable homes have better-funded local schools, better-paid teachers, better school facilities and more resources.

4:15 · Here’s a feedback loop: The better the schools in a neighborhood, the more those homes in that neighborhood are worth.

4:21 · And the higher the property values of those homes, the more money there is for schools.

4:25 · And so on and so on.

4:27 · And housing segregation in health.

4:29 · Because of urban planning that benefited those richer, whiter neighborhoods, people of color are more likely to live near industrial plants that spew toxic fumes; they’re more likely to live far away from grocery stores with fresh food, and in places where

the water isn’t drinkable.

HEALTH

4:43 · They’re more likely to live in neighborhoods with crumbling infrastructure, and in homes with toxic paint.

4:49 · Karen: When you’re living with rats, roaches, and things like that – that’s deplorable.

4:53 · You cannot have that kind of stuff with children running around in the building.

4:56 · A building that may be full of lead.

5:00 · And, not coincidentally, people of color have higher incidences of certain cancers, asthma and heart disease.

5:08 · And housing segregation in policing.

POLICING

5:11 · Housing segregation means we are having vastly different experiences with crime and vastly different experiences with policing.

5:17 · Because our neighborhoods are so segregated, sometimes racial profiling can be camouflaged as spatial profiling — where living in certain areas can make you more likely to be stopped by the police.

How “Third Places” Make Cities Healthier, Stronger

Martin Felsen - City Design, 10 02, 2025

Video (7:38)
Description

Cities can boost our health—when we feel like we belong. Explore how “third places” (neither home nor work) turn bricks and mortar into trust, ties, and well-being. From cafés and libraries to community centers and markets, see how everyday spaces compound into social capital—and why some cities now invest in third places first.

Watch to learn: - What “third places” are and why they matter for health and democracy - How small, low-stakes interactions build social capital - Why participation in clubs and associations has declined—and how design can counter it - How social prescribing links people to community groups - The U.S. Industrial Policy playbook: jobs → families → civic groups → trust in third place - The “third-place-first” strategy in cities beyond the U.S. and how quality of place attracts families and jobs - A tour of PILARES in Mexico City—how design + programming drive belonging and well-being - Practical examples of third place programs any city can host today

If you’re enjoying CityDesign, like, subscribe, and share to help more people discover how we shape cities—and how cities shape us.

Hashtags:

About me

Martin Felsen, FAIA, co-founded UrbanLab, an architecture and urban design firm in Chicago. Martin is a Fellow of the American Institute of Architects, and a Professor in the Illinois Institute of Technology’s (IIT, aka, Illinois Tech) College of Architecture. UrbanLab’s work synthesizes diverse design methodologies and technical innovations drawn equally from architecture and its complex urban and natural contexts. Built work to date includes houses, housing, mixed-use buildings, installations, and urban infrastructural projects. UrbanLab has received many design awards for projects across scales of production.

Transcript
The decline of civic ties

0:00 · Hi, I’m Martin Felson. Welcome to City Design, the channel where we explore how we shape cities and how cities shape us.

0:08 · Today’s question is, how do cities improve our health and well-being?

0:13 · Cities physically connect us. A first principle of city design is simple. We are not meant to be alone. We do much better when we share purpose in shared places. But today, our civic ties have thinned. Participation in clubs, associations, and congregations is way down. What’s at stake isn’t nostalgia.

0:34 · It’s social capital. The trust, the norms, and networks that help communities solve problems together. Why the decline in our physical connections, familiar forces, mobility uproots us, and screens capture our attention. As an urban designer, I also see an antidote.

The role of third places

0:54 · Brick and mortar third places. These are gathering spots that are neither home nor work. They’re where we swap ideas, organize, and belong. Cafes and barber shops, libraries and schools, faith halls and field houses. Third places normalize low stakes contact, and those weak ties add up to deliver enhanced well-being. They help us connect and cope together. Third places aren’t new.

1:22 · In the 1830s, Alexis Dtoqueville observed that Americans penchant for starting civic associations was a key factor to our unprecedented ability to make democracy work. He wrote that we’re forever forming a thousand different kinds of associations, every kind, large and small. What happens inside third places? They convert bricks and mortar into trust and ties. Physical capital into social capital. Their design matters, too.

How spaces build social capital

1:53 · Open, simple, yet versatile spaces instill a sense of ownership and group pride. Public libraries host book and hobby clubs, free classes, and meetups. Community centers host arts and fitness classes, neighborhood gatherings, and volunteer drives. Parks host walking groups, nature clubs, and community cleanups.

2:18 · City service offices host neighborhood associations, and block clubs. Houses of worship host service groups, support circles, and food pantries. Parishes, JCC’s, YMCA host wreck teams, community service projects, and family programming. Public schools host afterhour PTAs, youth clubs, and adult wreck leagues. Boys and girls clubs host teams, clubs, mentoring, and service projects.

2:48 · Clinics and health centers host mindfulness groups, caregiver classes, and peer support. Food banks host nutrition and cooking classes, and volunteer and service clubs. Maker spaces host hobby clubs, and skill and repair shares. Museums, galleries, and cultural centers host dosan programs, lectures, and arts clubs. Rec centers host leagues, pickup games, and volunteer coaching and referee training.

3:17 · Cafes and bars host book clubs, language tables, and interest group meetups.

3:23 · Co-working spaces host professional associations. Farmers markets host info booths, volunteer signups, and community campaigns. Different places, same effect. Regular contact, small commitments, real purpose. That’s how physical spaces compound into social capital and how social capital strengthens mental health and democratic life. Healthc care is catching up, too.

Policies for healthy cities

3:50 · Doctors and clinicians now use social prescribing, which are patient referrals to groups, classes, and caregivers circles. Because joining a third place group measurably improves our health.

4:03 · More broadly in the US, national public policies focus on jobs, families, and third places as direct paths to citizen and community well-being. Our industrial policy targets business sectors with incentives and penalties to raise job quantity and quality.

4:21 · Stabilizes families with home ownership and good jobs. channels family members into community organizations to spur civic participation, which finally deepens civic trust and well-being through participation in third places abroad.

A third place first strategy

4:40 · Some cities flip the order with a third place first strategy. Build third place social infrastructure. Catalyze networks of people and organizations that undergur local economies. Attract investment in jobs via quality of place.

4:56 · stabilize family and home as civic life strengthens. Let’s look at how this strategy works in practice. Polaris are small community centers cited across Mexico City. These are places to find free computers in internet, flexible classrooms, and hands-on workshops from carpentry to coding. Many include courtyards that flip from classes to festivals to civic meetings. Polaris work because sites are prioritized in underserved areas. Buildings are well-designed and easy to identify.

5:29 · Programs are free and ongoing. In Ketal Kowal, this Polaris offers educational and practical support to rebuild social ties and safety within a dicey neighborhood. Classrooms and workshops open onto a shared courtyard and the operable facade signals that the space is open to all and available for everyday use and community ownership. In ease to Palapa on a tight site with little open space, the entry plaza and column threshold pulls the street inside the Polaris.

Case study: Polaris centers

6:02 · Simple materials, strided block, concrete tile, steel create light, shade and durable rooms that flex from forum to classroom. In qui Quilo, a slender steel frame shades the interior spaces of this neighborhood hub. The inverted roof captures rainwater architecture doing double duty in a water stressed city. In La Pula, this educational center has a single unified room on two levels.

6:31 · The large multi-purpose space offers free training workshops of all kinds for everyone in the neighborhood. In Valentine Gomez FAS, this Polaris is filled with naturally lit classrooms linked to a public walkway with lattice walls and gardens used for learning and neighborhood life. Free classes, workshops, and outdoor forums entice people of all ages to gather, learn, and belong. The bottom line here is that third places aren’t a luxury.

Innovation in belonging

7:01 · They’re our everyday infrastructure of connection and well-being. Design them well. Program them predictably. Open them to everyone. The benefits compound.

7:14 · We talk a lot about innovation in technology. Here’s another kind.

7:18 · Innovation in belonging. Cities that invest in it will be healthier, safer, and more confident about their future.

7:26 · Thanks for watching City Design. If you’re enjoying these episodes, please like, share, and subscribe.

How America’s hottest city is trying to cool down

Vox, 09 20, 2021

Video (6:48)
Description

Can trees help save Phoenix from extreme heat?

Subscribe and turn on notifications 🔔 so you don’t miss any videos: http://goo.gl/0bsAjO

It’s time to stop looking at trees as a form of “beautification.” They are, instead, a living form of infrastructure, providing a variety of services that include stormwater management, air filtering, carbon sequestration, and, most importantly for a city like Phoenix, Arizona, they cool the environment around them.

Trees can lower neighborhood temperatures in three ways: 1) Their shade prevents solar radiation from hitting paved surfaces like concrete and asphalt, which absorb energy and rerelease it into the air as heat. 2) Their leaves pull heat from the immediate area in order to evapotranspirate water that’s drawn from the soil. And, 3) If you’re standing under one, a tree protects your body directly from the sun’s rays. If you’ve ever made a summer visit to a dry, hot city like Phoenix, you’ll know how important shade is for making any outdoor experiences tolerable.

As Phoenix deals with a rising frequency of extreme heat waves — which aren’t only deadly, but also cause worrisome spikes in energy demand — the city is looking to trees as part of its heat mitigation strategy. Phoenix isn’t devoid of trees, but they’re distributed unevenly across the city. A quick glance at a satellite image of the metro area reveals substantial green splotches in the north and east and brown ones in the south and west, where many lower-income neighborhoods are located.

So Phoenix recently pledged to reach “tree equity” by 2030, under an agreement with American Forests, a national tree organization. I visited Phoenix recently to take a look at the current state of the city’s urban forest. In this video, we use drone imagery and thermal cameras to understand how the urban design of the city contributes to extreme heat, and what it can do to cool down.

This is the first video of five videos we’re releasing on climate change. You can watch the second video, about high-voltage transmission lines ⚡️ and why the US isn’t ready for clean energy, here: https://youtu.be/s3ScJ_FwaZk

And the third video dives into prescribed burns, and how a decade of suppressing forest fires 🔥 may have made them worse, here: https://youtu.be/0o6ezu_h6iE

How Do You Share a Shrinking River Fairly

PBS, 09 10, 2026

Video (8:53)
Description

Watch more of this series: https://to.pbs.org/4wkQIAG

The Colorado River is running out — and the Imperial Valley is ground zero. As policymakers battle over rights to a shrinking river, farmers are grappling with the practical realities of growing food with less water. Miles O’Brien meets two Imperial Valley farmers who are finding ways to feed people and livestock, nearby and abroad, while trying to make good use of every drop of this hard-working river.

Resolve to Solve with Miles O’Brien

Miles O’Brien travels the globe searching for solutions to climate, water, and health crises. From building sea curtains in Antarctica to restoring wildlife in Argentina, the answers are closer than we think thanks to people with a “Resolve to Solve.”

0:08 · Together, they act as a giant savings account, buffering water users from the whims of weather and the uncertainty of the annual snowpack.

1:31 · I am fourth-generation, and my son is fifth-generation.

1:34 · We are very, very proud of that fact.

1:36 · O’BRIEN (voiceover): Gina is also a director on the board of the Imperial Irrigation District– the public agency that holds and manages the single largest entitlement to water from the Colorado River.

1:48 · Besides citrus, her family grows dates and, like just about everyone here, alfalfa and Bermuda grass, both of which get bundled up into hay bales to be fed to livestock.

2:02 · You can’t put all your eggs in one basket, right?

2:04 · Otherwise, how do you make it from year to year?

2:05 · O’BRIEN: No crop demands more Colorado River water than alfalfa.

2:10 · Farmers across the basin use roughly five to six million acre-feet a year to grow hay for cattle and dairy operations.

2:19 · The Imperial Valley is one of the world’s most productive hay-growing regions.

2:23 · Thanks to a year-round growing season and easy access to Pacific ports, as much as half of its alfalfa is exported to Asia and the Middle East– controversial destinations for a crop irrigated by one of America’s most stressed rivers.

3:11 · O’BRIEN: Alfalfa is a thirsty crop, and the fact that a significant share of it ultimately leaves the country doesn’t sit well with many people.

3:21 · But Gina says folks in the Imperial Valley are accustomed to being in the crosshairs.

3:27 · DOCKSTADER: We’ve always felt that other people were looking at our water because we have such a significant… priority right.

3:34 · You think municipalities are gonna come in, you think the cities are gonna come and, and take our water.

Water management and policy

3:40 · O’BRIEN: That’s exactly what happened in 2003.

3:43 · As it became clear the Colorado River could no longer meet all the demands placed on it, the federal government required California to live within its legal allocation.

3:55 · The result was the Quantification Settlement Agreement, or QSA.

4:00 · It requires the Imperial Irrigation District to transfer water to San Diego.

4:06 · In return, the San Diego County Water Authority helps fund conservation projects that enable farmers to use less water while keeping much of their land in production.

4:18 · DOCKSTADER: Now I can pay for a sprinkler pipe.

4:20 · I can sprinkle, I can use less water to grow the same crop, and that’s how the water gets created.

4:27 · We’re getting smarter.

4:30 · They, we all know we have to do more with less.

Adapting to a limited supply

How FIVE BILLION Pounds of Las Vegas Garbage Powers a City

PBS Terra, 04 20, 2021

Video (9:14)
Description

PBS Member Stations rely on viewers like you. To support your local station, go to: http://to.pbs.org/DonateTerra

Celebrate Earth Day with our friends at PBS: https://bit.ly/3elpV1w

Head over to Reactions to find out more about how they’re celebrating Earth Day, and tell them Joe sent you! https://youtu.be/I1YLPfSuNXY

Most of the 600 billion pounds of waste that Americans produce every year ends up in landfills. All that trash can have huge impacts on the environment. But modern landfills have found a new use for all that trash — they’re turning it into energy. In spite of their reputation as “dumps,” these landfills are feats of engineering, more akin to construction sites.

One of North America’s biggest landfills lies on the outskirts of Las Vegas. The Apex Landfill is not only one of the country’s largest, it’s also one of the busiest. Because it serves a non-stop city, the landfill must operate 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, 365 days a year. It receives upwards of 16 million pounds of trash per day or 5 billion pounds per year.

Landfills like Apex are required to deal with the toxic chemicals they produce, like methane, a greenhouse gas that’s 84 times more potent than carbon dioxide. At Apex, they capture that methane and turn it into energy that powers 11,000 homes in southern Nevada.

Subscribe to PBS Terra! - https://bit.ly/3mOfd77

Hosted by Joe Hanson from It’s Okay to be Smart, Overview uses incredible 4k drone footage to reveal the natural phenomena shaping our planet from a 10,000-foot view—literally.

Transcript
Intro

0:02 · [Host Joe Hanson] Americans produce 4.9 pounds of waste per person per day. That’s nearly 600 billion pounds per year.

0:11 · Where does it all go?

0:13 · It goes to places like this. The mountains of trash we throw away can have huge impacts on our environment and climate.

0:23 · But what if I told you that all of this waste could one day power a city?

0:29 · [synth music] ♪ [Joe] Welcome to Las Vegas, the place for glitz, glam, gambling and garbage. Three main categories of waste are solid waste, recyclables, and food waste. And here in the neon city, we’re going to explore the ways they’re turning each of these trash types into treasure. Las Vegas produces more than five billion pounds of waste per year, and all that trash ends up here. The Apex Landfill lies in the mountains beyond the city.

Apex Landfill

1:12 · At 1900 acres, it’s one of the largest landfills in North America, and also one of the busiest. Apex is one of the only landfills in North America that runs 24 hours a day, seven days a week, 365 days a year. As many as 250 trucks enter the landfill each day and deliver up to 16 million pounds of waste. It used to be a place like this was called a dump, and that’s exactly what they were.

1:46 · trash dumped in piles with little regard for sanitation. As trash decays, it produces methane, a powerful greenhouse gas. The dumps of yesteryear all but ignored this, as well as other environmental problems. But today’s landfills are feats of engineering. They are long-term storehouses for society’s garbage and places where we manage its potential hazards.

2:14 · [David Vossmer]: It would be comparable to a construction site, where you’re building homes in a neighborhood. We would envision an entire city being built basically as a landfill.

2:26 · [Joe]: David Vossmer has been working in the solid waste industry for 42 years and oversees operations at Apex.

Working Phase

2:33 · [David]: The working face is the active area of the landfill, usually anywhere from two to three acres in size.

2:41 · [Joe]: Each truck that dumps its load carries about 30 tons of garbage. Compactors then take that trash, spread it across the working face, and mash it down.

2:57 · [David]: Each one of those machines is about 120 to 130,000 pounds. There’s a lot of weight that will smash all the cardboard boxes or trash or any other material that comes in. It’ll lay it down in a nice, even layer. That’s what the landfill business is trying to do, get as much compacted waste into that area or that acre that we can. That’s what extends the life of the landfill.

3:24 · [Joe]: As more and more trash comes in, the landfill grows in height.

3:29 · [David]: It’s just like building a pyramid. The wider the base, the higher we can go with the trash here in the landfill.

3:36 · [Joe]: In some areas, the local landfill is the highest point in the region. Here in Vegas, this mountain of trash is 500 feet high and rising taller by the day. In spite of the enormous volume of garbage coming in, the landfill will be able to take in trash for another 300 plus years.

3:57 · How is that possible?

4:01 · Not only is the site large, but it’s also growing. A mining company on site digs out the surrounding mountains. In the process, it expands the landfill’s footprint and the space it has to operate. But the best way to keep a landfill from filling up is to waste less. Las Vegas boasts the largest residential recycling center in North America. The state-of-the-art facility takes in up to 1.8 million pounds of recyclables per day.

Recycling

4:32 · Because Las Vegas uses single stream recycling, all the sorting happens here. These recyclables will get conveyed through a complex system of sorting machines.

4:45 · [Jeremy Walters]: We have some very unique pieces of equipment, things that do just simple mechanical separation through disks and screens, but we also have computerized machines that are physically reading the material based on its color and density. It’s very smart, and it’s very quick. After a machine initially separates material, people quality control what the machine did.

5:10 · They’re physically looking at the material to ensure that the machine sorted correctly and there are no contaminants within that final product.

5:19 · [Joe]: A new challenge confronting recycling centers like this is the Amazon effect. Facilities around the country are being inundated with cardboard from online retailers. Here at this facility, they’ve had to recalibrate their machines and processes just to handle the deluge. While 1.8 million pounds of daily recyclables might sound like a lot, it’s still just a fraction of the overall waste that gets created each day.

5:49 · Food is another thing that inundates the waste stream and doesn’t belong in a landfill. Las Vegas is renowned buffets produce a lot of it. But here in Sin City, they’ve found an innovative solution. It’s not just people who pig out on buffets. The residents of the Las Vegas Livestock Farm enjoy it too. The farm sits on Apex property, but is family-owned.

6:17 · [Hank Combs]: Hog farming in Nevada is not very popular, because of the access to feed. We’ve circumvented that by doing the food scrap route, which is a very sustainable way to raise our hogs.

6:28 · [Joe]: They take in up to 40,000 pounds per day of the casinos’ food waste. Everything from lobster to ice cream gets processed in giant cookers to make it safe for the hogs to eat. This fragrant stew won’t make the menu in any casino, but it’s irresistible to these hogs.

Food Waste

6:48 · I mean, yummy.

6:50 · [Hank]: They’re a lot like a human, so they love their sweets and their meat and the potatoes. They’re not too big on salads. They won’t eat anything. They’re picky.

7:00 · [Joe]: It’s not just food waste that’s finding a second life in Vegas. The garbage is too. In the U.S., landfills like this account for nearly 20% of the human-caused methane emissions. Some landfills capture and burn it. But here at Apex, and at a growing number of landfills around the country, they’re turning it into energy. 160 wells have been drilled into this mountain of trash, some as deep as 200 feet.

7:31 · The wells siphon off the gas coming from landfill. After it’s purified, it’s sent to an onsite power plant where it’s burned to spin turbines, which create energy. That energy is fed back into the electric grid and powers 11,000 homes here in Southern Nevada. The total amount of energy produced annually by U.S. landfills powers the equivalent of more than 1 million homes.

7:56 · [Jeremy]: We’re actually able to take something that is always going to exist in a landfill, and turn it into something that the community can benefit from. Most people go day to day without thinking about the trash or the recyclables that they make. It’s just a simple toss it in the bin and forget about it.

8:10 · And there’s so much involved behind the scenes to make sure that we are handling all those materials in the most environmentally responsible way.

8:20 · [David]: Not everything in our world is recyclable. And as long as society throws things away, we’re one of the things that take care of making sure it’s done the right way.

8:33 · [Joe]: Hey guys, our PBS friends across YouTube are celebrating Earth Day with us. Follow me over to Reactions to find out why catalytic converters are being stolen from cars worldwide, and what this weird mystery has to do with the health of our environment. Tell them Joe sent you.

How highways make traffic worse

Vox, 02 12, 2021

Video (6:04)
Description

Expanding highways doesn’t do what you think it does.

Subscribe and turn on notifications (🔔 ) so you don’t miss any videos: http://goo.gl/0bsAjO

Big, expensive highway expansion projects are the source of a lot US transportation funding — but they aren’t a silver bullet for congestion relief. In communities that were built for cars, solving traffic problems requires much more holistic problem-solving.

At 1:00, we show a bar graph of travel times on the Katy Freeway that was originally put together by City Observatory, which has covered the Katy Freeway expansion project at length:

https://cityobservatory.org/reducing-congestion-katy-didnt/

This video was based in large part on research by Gilles Duranton and Matthew A. Turner:

https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/aer.101.6.2616

For more reading on induced demand:

https://www.wired.com/2014/06/wuwt-traffic-induced-demand/

https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2018-09-06/traffic-jam-blame-induced-demand?sref=PxYB8Mnq

For Kyle Shelton’s work on urbanism:

https://kinder.rice.edu/urban-edge/author/541

Vox.com is a news website that helps you cut through the noise and understand what’s really driving the events in the headlines. Check out http://www.vox.com.

Watch our full video catalog: http://goo.gl/IZONyE

Follow Vox on Facebook: http://goo.gl/U2g06o

Or Twitter: http://goo.gl/XFrZ5H

Transcript
The Katy Freeway’s scale

0:01 · The Katy Freeway in Texas connects Houston’s western suburbs with the city’s downtown.

0:08 · At its widest point, right here, it spans 26 lanes including parallel roads, before it intersects with another freeway, creating this massive web of pavement. The Katy Freeway is among the widest in the world. But it didn’t start out this big. The freeway was initially built in the 1960’s with 6 lanes in most places. But as the suburbs and office space around Houston started growing in the 1980’ s and 90’s and more people began using the freeway— it became a traffic nightmare. By 2004, it was ranked the second worst bottleneck in the country.

Expansion and continued traffic

0:40 · To accommodate the growing commuter class, the city began a nearly 3 billion dollar expansion project, to add the additional lanes. The solution seems natural — more lanes equals less congestion. But traffic didn’t get any better. In fact, it got worse, in both the morning and afternoon commutes.

Economic theory of traffic

1:02 · The reason why hinges on a simple economic theory. One that is often overlooked, because actually reducing traffic is far from simple. Highway expansion has gone hand in hand with the suburbanization of American cities like Houston. It becomes a self-fulfilling recipe for urban sprawl: a highway gets built to connect suburbs to a city center, which encourages more development along it, which necessitates even more highways when those get congested — and on and on and on.

1:33 · The instinct to widen highways to relieve traffic makes sense—but there’s a reason it doesn’t work: due to a concept called “induced demand.” These represent 3 highway lanes. And these balls are the commuters that drive on them. These particular commuters — the red ones — will sit in traffic no matter how bad it gets, because they have to. Driving to work on the highway is their only option. Let’s say this is what congestion looks like, during peak rush hours. Once a certain number of cars get on the highway, traffic slows to a crawl. Now let’s add a new lane.

Understanding induced demand

2:04 · These drivers now have more room to spread out — which should make traffic flow better. That might happen at first, but it doesn’t stay that way. That’s because there’s another set of people who will take the highway under the right conditions — even though they have other commuting options. When a highway is congested, they might take local roads instead. Or be able to drive during off-peak hours. They might use other modes of transportation, like public transit or biking.

2:34 · Or maybe they can work from home that day and skip the commute altogether. In a few years, these people will start taking the highway, enticed by less congestion. This is induced demand at play: the more supply there is, the more demand will follow, to exhaustion. And in this case, the supply is highway lanes. And sometimes, like on the Katy freeway, congestion gets even worse after a highway expansion, until some of those people with more options go back to their old ways. But in the end, you’re still left with more drivers, and congestion that’s at least as bad as it was before.

3:02 · When our transportation system is so reliant on highways and private automobiles, there’s almost no way around it because that’s the system that we’ve created. This is Kyle Shelton, an urbanist based in Houston. The endless reduction of congestion… should that be…the driving, honestly the driving policy question for a lot of our transportation funding? Big expensive highway infrastructure projects are still the prevailing band-aid to congestion in the US.

Challenges to the system

3:32 · The transit advocacy group Transportation for America found that between 1993 and 2017, the US added over 30,000 miles of new freeway lanes in 100 metro areas. Building more highways may provide some short-term relief. And it’s easier than most infrastructure projects to get federal funding to do a highway expansion. But if we want less traffic and fewer drivers, giving flexible commuters better choices is a good place to start. Like by improving public transit by adding more and better bus routes or trains.

4:06 · That alone might not be a silver bullet for congestion relief, for the same reason that adding another lane isn’t: new drivers will take the place of transit commuters on the highway. And for many people living off highways in sprawling US cities, public transit may never be an adequate solution.

4:23 · ‘Cause it’s not just about the infrastructure. It’s also about individual behaviors. It’s about where job opportunities are located. And most of our cities have now been constructed in this way where the car is the prime mode. Another option is to enact policies that actively disincentivize people from using the highway. Like congestion pricing, which charges people who drive on highways during rush hours. Or remote work programs that deter people from traveling during the highest traffic times — or make it so they don’t have to commute at all.

Alternative solutions

4:54 · And in the long-term, better land use policies can help as well, like by building communities that put people closer to where they need to go. And if building more highways results in more drivers and congestion, then removing them could have the opposite effect.

Highway removal and future

5:10 · For example, the city of Boston removed a freeway in its city center in the 1990s, and replaced it with a boulevard with biking and bus lanes and more space to walk. It reduced congestion by 62%. And now the Democratically controlled Senate is considering nearly $10 billion in funding for similar highway-removal projects in other cities. What we build and invest in in the world of transportation truly changes our behavior.

5:38 · If building more roads makes us drive on them more. Then giving people better choices by investing in the right things, will make us drive less. Because, if we build it, they will come.

How redlining prevented Black and Brown families from becoming home owners

Harvard Kennedy School, 09 19, 2023

Video (4:28)
Description

The term “redlining” refers to the practice by banks of excluding Black and Brown Americans from receiving loans to buy homes and make improvements to their communities. Redlining arose during the Great Depression, when the federal government sought to boost homeownership by encouraging banks to lend to more Americans. Many neighborhoods, specifically those with majority Black and Brown residents, were deemed undeserving of these loans. Though redlining was made illegal by the Fair Housing Act, the effects of this practice still reverberate to this day.

In this video, Khalil Gibran Muhammad, Ford Foundation Professor of History, Race, and Public Policy at Harvard Kennedy School and director of the Institutional Antiracism and Accountability Project, provides background on the history and legacy of redlining.

About Harvard Kennedy School:

The John F. Kennedy School of Government at Harvard University is a graduate and professional school that brings together students, scholars, and practitioners who combine thought and action to make the world a better place.

Our mission is to improve public policy and public leadership across the United States and around the world so that people can lead safer, freer, and more prosperous lives. Harvard Kennedy School teaches current and future leaders the skills they need to effectively advance the public purpose in the public, nonprofit, and private sectors. Our renowned faculty and trailblazing research centers pioneer bold new ideas. And as the most international school at Harvard, we convene global leaders in the Forum, host visiting experts in the classroom, and attract a diverse community of faculty, students, and staff.

Transcript

0:00 · In every way imaginable, the consequences of redlining to many black and brown communities across America meant that those communities had the least and the last of everything.

0:16 · So I want to talk about redlining, because this is a term you may have heard, but most people don’t actually know the history.

0:24 · In 1933, in the midst of America’s Great Depression, when unemployment rates were 25% and millions of people were not only out of work, but many of them were houseless, the federal government under President Franklin Delano Roosevelt established an agency called the Home Owners Loan Corporation.

0:42 · Basically, it tried to make home buying much more affordable by subsidizing the cost of building and lending such that people would be able to afford to buy for the first time.

0:55 · Millions of Americans participated, except that when the Home Owners Loan Corporation began to issue mortgages, it came up with a scheme to decide which communities were deserving of loans and which ones weren’t.

1:10 · They made maps and used a color coded scheme.

1:14 · Green meant this was a community that you could lend to and red you could not.

1:19 · The basic decision they made was to determine that any community with the presence of black people or brown people or people who, perhaps, spoke Italian, in certain parts of the country could not receive support from the Home Owners Loan Corporation.

1:36 · This created a system that came to be known as redlining because communities that were deemed risky by the mere presence of people of color, most especially black people, were disqualified from getting direct support from the federal government to purchase homes.

1:53 · This policy lasted until 1968, when the federal government passed the Fair Housing Act, which made all forms of discrimination in the buying and selling or renting of homes illegal.

2:08 · But the truth is that the legacies of redlining from that moment to the present meant that black people were subjected to other forms of exploitative lending.

2:18 · A system called contract buying grew up as a way to sell black people homes on a layaway plan.

2:26 · You made set payments over an extended period of time, but you never owned the home until the very last payment.

2:34 · It was very common for unscrupulous sellers to withhold that final payment in an effort to take back the home from a person who had worked incredibly hard to buy it.

2:45 · Home ownership has been the most important asset that a typical white family has in order to do simple things like borrow money to send a child to college.

2:58 · But most importantly, they have financial freedom.

3:01 · But for communities that have been subjected to redlining, they didn’t have those advantages.

3:08 · Not only that, the very communities that they lived in suffered from divestment, including the lack of grocery stores, the lack of businesses, the imposition of federal highways that often bisected their communities.

3:24 · In every way imaginable, the consequences of redlining to many black and brown communities across America meant that those communities had the least and the last of everything.

3:38 · And to this day, the median wages and income of those communities, and the financial insecurity that people who live in redlined communities face, has long term health consequences for families, has educational consequences for young people whose schools often don’t have the tax basis to give them the same resources that communities that were never redlined actually have.

Transcript
Intro

0:01 · No joke, but this place…

0:02 · has a serious issue with water.

0:06 · Water here has changed the course of war, started fights with neighboring countries, and dominates the city’s political agenda.

0:14 · And yet, this country is a role model.

0:18 · “Singapore got it right, as simple as that.”

0:20 · This is how Singapore is transforming itself from one of the most water-stressed countries in the world to self-sufficiency, from water rags – to riches.

The challenge

0:36 · Welcome to Singapore!

0:37 · A vibrant multicultural city-state, right on the equator.

0:41 · Densely populated, around 6 million people live on this tiny island.

0:45 · It’s an international hub for trade and finance.

0:48 · It’s clean, safe, modern, wealthy, green.

0:52 · Basically, it has a lot of everything you’d want.

0:55 · There’s just that one thing…

0:56 · Singapore has no natural freshwater resources.

1:00 · And the way its economy and population are growing, total water demand could almost double by 2060.

1:06 · But Singapore is on it.

1:10 · “None of what they’ve done is magic.”

1:13 · That’s Peter Gleick, he’s an award-winning water expert.

1:16 · He puts Singapore’s success down to what he calls the “soft path” approach to their problems.

1:21 · “So the soft path for water is in contrast to what we have done over the last century and more, more than a century, the hard path.

1:29 · To build hard infrastructure, to take more and more water out of nature, to ignore the consequences of our water policies for nature, to build narrow institutions.

1:39 · And the soft path tries to turn that around and say, let’s use water efficiently and carefully.

1:45 · Let’s stop wasting water.

1:47 · Let’s look at new sources of supply.”

1:50 · To understand how Singapore can pull this off, you first need to understand where they’re coming from.

History

1:58 · “The Singapore water story starts with World War 2.”

2:02 · That’s Jon Church, the guy for water at the United Nations.

2:06 · Singaporeans would argue that the story goes back a lot longer, but 1942 is certainly when the issue grabbed the world’s attention.

2:13 · That’s when allied troops, namely British, Australian and Indian forces, were battling fascist Japan on Singapore Island, which at the time was a British colony.

2:24 · The allies depended on imported water which was a bit of a problem when Japanese forces blew up the pipes transporting that water.

2:30 · “The bridge that connects Malaysia and Singapore was bombed.

2:35 · The result was lack of water in the city, a terrible episode of water scarcity.”

2:43 · The Allies lost the battle of Singapore, but after Japan’s overall surrender, the island remained in British hands.

2:50 · It took more than 20 years until it became fully independent.

2:53 · But political liberation didn’t free Singapore from its water crisis: water rationing, catastrophic sanitation, and regular floods continued.

3:01 · With its fate now in its own hands, Singapore began planning for the long-term.

3:06 · Cecilia Tortajada has spent almost three decades researching water policy and innovations around the world and is fascinated by Singapore’s path.

3:15 · “When Singapore became independent, they started planning to be water independent, as well as food independent, energy independent, but to have systems that can sustain stress.

3:28 · That was in 1965 for 2060.”

Step 1: Imported Water

3:32 · Their initial masterplan was fine-tuned over the years into a water strategy which they call their “4 national taps”.

3:40 · First: Water imports Second: Desalination Third: Local Catchment And fourth, something they call “NEWater”.

3:50 · Let’s dive into it!

3:53 · Firstly, Singapore knew there was plenty of water, right here: Two deals to import water from Malaysia in the 60’s, got the taps running again.

4:03 · It’s cheap and millions of liters are pumped over the border every day.

4:07 · But buying half your water from your neighbor isn’t sustainable long-term.

4:12 · On the contrary: From the start, Malaysia made threats to cut off the supply and argued over its price.

4:18 · The tensions have even led to warnings of a military conflict.

4:21 · Singapore’s leaders know their weak spot, so they want to stop importing water by 2061.

4:27 · So, it’s all the more important that the other three taps become more than a drop in the ocean.

4:31 · “Water planning is very important because they have so little water, Singapore must make sure, that this water is used wisely.

4:41 · And the objective of this master plan is to make the most out of every single drop of water.”

4:48 · This means keeping rivers and drains clean, investing billions, starting to collect more water, cleaning it and use what the island state Singapore already has.

Step 2: Desalination

4:57 · For example, this: The ocean!

5:02 · “Desalination, Desalination, Desalination.

5:05 · You take that undrinkable salt water, you remove the salt and you have an unlimited supply of fresh water.”

5:11 · Do you remember?

5:12 · We had an entire video about obtaining fresh water through desalination.

5:16 · It’s used in a number of extremely dry places around the world and is a real gamechanger for some.

5:23 · “Membrane desalination uses pressure.

5:25 · Salt water, here coloured in red for clarity, is pressed through a membrane that is only partially permeable.

5:30 · Fresh water can press through.

5:32 · Here coloured in blue.

5:33 · But the salt is trapped on the other side.”

5:35 · Singapore really pushed to advance this technology.

5:38 · This underground facility for example is state-of-the-art.

5:42 · Normally, it treats used water.

5:44 · In times of drought, it desalinates sea water.

5:47 · On top, people use it as a park.

5:49 · Today, five desalination plants provide up to 25 % of the entire island’s water supply.

5:55 · Singapore plans increase this capacity to meet 30% of its needs in 2060, by which time water use is expected to have doubled.

6:04 · But that’s no way near self-sufficiency.

6:07 · So, what’s next?

Step 3: Local Catchment

6:09 · Bingo! Rain!

6:11 · A lot of it, and Singapore is a master of maxing that out.

6:15 · Two third of the entire state’s surface is used for rainwater catchment.

6:20 · “Basically, the water falls on the roof and then goes through drains and then you make sure that as little water leaks from the drains and is captured by the drainage system and conveyed to reservoirs where it can be stored.

6:43 · And treated for further use.

6:46 · An extensive network of rivers, canals and drains channels the water into 17 reservoirs.

6:51 · The biggest is Marina Barrage, with an area of 10,000 hectares.

6:55 · It holds back fresh water from flowing into the ocean.

6:58 · And helps to control frequent floods.

7:02 · So does this underground tank that catches floodwater in extreme cases when the drains spill over.

7:08 · Even this water could potentially be treated and reused.

7:11 · By 2060, the government wants to use 90% of the land area for rain catchment.

Step 4: NEWater

7:18 · Catching rainwater is one thing, but what about the water already in circulation?

7:25 · “All drainage water is collected, and treated and reused as much as possible.

7:32 · Most countries, they do not invest, not even a fraction of what Singapore is investing.”

7:38 · The water authorities built a 206 kilometer sewage pipe-highway, costing 10 billion dollars that guides the city’s sewage into state-of-the-art reclamation and cleaning facilities.

7:50 · Ok, Singapore is by some measures the 5th richest country in the world so it can afford to splash out like that.

7:56 · It’s also a lot easier to push through such projects when you have the sort of “controlled democracy”, run by the same party, that Singapore has had since independence in 1965.

8:07 · Anyway, the entire city’s underground is basically one big sewer network.

8:12 · But the pride of Singapore’s water strategy is what happens after collecting the water – the treatment.

8:19 · The authorities call it NEWater.

8:21 · It’s produced by microfiltration, reverse osmosis and UV radiation.

8:29 · “Some of that water is so high quality, Singapore is using it in their chip manufacturing industry, which requires ultra-pure water, which is an indication of how good a quality of that water is.”

8:42 · Did you know, that around the world, half of our wastewater is released untreated?

8:46 · And only 11% is actually reused.

8:49 · In Singapore about 30% percent of the entire drinkable and non-drinkable demand can be met by recycling used water.

8:57 · And they want to increase that to 55% by 2060.

9:02 · Most of it is used by industry, only a fraction of it is mixed into the drinking water supply, because we’re all so squeamish.

9:09 · “It’s controversial because we’re taking wastewater which, you know, goes down our drains, we flush it down our toilets, industry dumps wastewater.

9:17 · And we typically think of that as a, a liability, as something to get rid of.”

Policy and Education

9:22 · So how do you get people on board?

9:25 · “Using the flush saver cistern bag and save with every flush!”

9:29 · “Make saving water pay!”

9:30 · “Reduce water consumption!”

9:32 · “Save up to 10 liters of water per hour!”

9:35 · Nationwide campaigns encourage people to install water-saving fittings.

9:38 · And nicely, if you install those fittings, you get discount vouchers for other sustainable products.

9:44 · Digital water meters track each household’s water consumption and detect leaks in pipes.

9:49 · That’s how Singapore comes down to an incredible 5% water loss from leaks.

9:53 · Which is first class.

9:55 · Globally, the average is estimated to be 30%.

9:58 · “What they’ve done incredibly well, in my opinion, is on the side of water education.

10:04 · They’ve educated their community about their water situation, about their water challenges, and about the solutions that they’ve chosen to push.”

Conclusion

10:14 · As good as Singapore is doing, it has big advantages over other countries.

10:18 · Besides being rich and a tightly-controlled society, the city only has a tiny agricultural sector and can focus almost entirely on urban and industrial wastewater.

10:29 · So, they have one problem less as food production pollutes and consumes enormous amounts of fresh water in many parts of the world.

10:36 · Despite that, they’ve shown: a lot is possible.

10:41 · “Everywhere in the world, when we start, again talking about water - when we see our management, how can it be improved?

10:50 · Who would be involved?

10:52 · How can we pay for it?

10:54 · There is always a “but”.

10:55 · “But” can we do it?

10:56 · And in Singapore it’s not.

10:58 · In Singapore it’s: how is it that we are going to do it?

11:01 · So, it’s a very different perspective, its proactive.

11:06 · They move very fast.

11:08 · So once a decision has been taken the things start happening.”

11:14 · So, to sum up: Incentivizing low-cost water-saving fittings could be easy for every government to implement.

11:20 · Desalination is only an option for coastal regions and it requires a lot of energy, often dirty fossil fuels.

11:27 · Singapore’s catchment, treatment and purification facilities are world class, as the result of a lot of investment in innovation and research.

11:34 · “But it turns out that a dollar invested in an efficiency improvement is much more productive than a dollar invested in new supply.”

11:45 · Reusing wastewater seems a no-brainer.

11:47 · It’s safe and tested to work and the tech is available.

11:52 · “This is really important to find the best solutions to every country’s problems, but also long-term planning.

12:01 · Singapore, from all the way from independence has been planning its way through water security.

12:09 · In Singapore it’s extremely high on the political agenda, all the way up to the Prime Minister.

12:16 · It’s something which is mainstreamed in each and every policy adopted and implemented by the country.”

12:25 · Singapore is blazing a trail in tackling some of the world’s biggest water challenges in the face of climate change.

12:30 · It’s not just about money, but also about decision-making, policy and long-term planning.

12:35 · Some of the ingredients with which any region could make it from water rags to riches.

How systemic racism shaped the ecosystems of U.S. cities

Science Magazine, 10 09, 2020

Video (4:08)
Description

Historically Black and immigrant communities are more vulnerable to environmental stressors

Read the research: https://scim.ag/3nzjnQE

music

“Vultures” by Chris Burns

Transcript

0:01 · The urban environment is a feat of human decision-making— from where to develop street grids lined with large glass office buildings, to which green spaces to preserve for outdoor recreation.

0:13 · How humans make these choices, and the natural environment’s response, can create extremely different ecosystems in neighborhoods just a few blocks away from each other.

0:23 · Researchers delved into dozens of studies to understand what drives these variations.

0:29 · One well documented phenomenon in cities is the relationship between wealth and biodiversity.

0:35 · More affluent areas generally have greater canopy cover, with larger, mature trees, as well as a higher diversity of birds.

0:45 · This is known as the “luxury effect.”

0:48 · Low-income areas typically have more man-made surfaces— including major heat-absorbers like asphalt and concrete, compared to higher-income areas.

0:59 · The lack of shade from trees and vegetation, combined with more asphalt and concrete, makes it hotter in these neighborhoods— a phenomenon known as an “urban heat island.”

1:10 · These communities are also more likely to be near sources of air pollutants, like expansive interstates pumping car exhaust.

1:19 · Although wealth can sometimes predict the outcomes of an urban ecosystem, there isn’t always a clear relationship.

1:26 · In some cases, the racial make-up of a neighborhood is better than income when forecasting canopy cover.

1:33 · Researchers explored studies that highlight how systemic racism shaped our build environment.

1:39 · One glaring example in the United States is residential segregation.

1:44 · From 1933-1968, the federal government limited access to homeownership among Black Americans through a practice known as redlining.

1:55 · Neighborhoods were graded based on the riskiness of providing a mortgage in the area.

2:00 · The grades ranged from A, the most desirable areas, full of wealthy businessmen, to D, neighborhoods considered high-risk investments due to a combination of factors: from their environmental quality and distance from large industrial factories to the main determinant, the presence of foreign-born and Black people.

2:22 · The inability for Black people to buy homes in these neighborhoods meant many types of capital investments left— landlords abandoned their properties, and public services, such as transportation and park maintenance, weren’t prioritized.

2:36 · Today, many U.S. cities still exhibit long-lasting environmental impacts from this discrimination.

2:42 · Neighborhoods which had a “D” grade in the 60s have about half the canopy cover of historically white communities.

2:50 · Some studies evaluate how the current environment relates to historically redlined communities, but researchers did not find any research that traces how ecosystems changed over time because of this segregation.

3:03 · They propose that because habitable regions are more spread out in these areas, animal populations struggle to breed since they are cut off from each other.

3:14 · The reduced breeding options for animals could have decreased gene diversity, an important way for animals to adapt to changing environments.

3:23 · And decreased gene flow of native species could promote the abundance of pest species, like mosquitos and brown rats, which carry diseases that can infect humans.

3:34 · The combination of all these outcomes— from urban heat islands to increased pests— make low-income, marginalized communities far more vulnerable to risks like climate change.

3:47 · Scientists say such evidence shows that conservation and social justice cross paths— especially along neighborhood streets.

How the US made affordable homes illegal

Vox, 08 16, 2021

Video (9:41)
Description

The rules that keep American housing expensive.

Subscribe and turn on notifications (🔔) so you don’t miss any videos: http://goo.gl/0bsAjO

Over the past year, housing prices in the US rose precipitously. Low interest rates and millennials’ entry into the market spiked demand across the nation, leading housing prices in some cities to increase by more than 20 percent in one year, and crushing the dreams of many would-be homeowners.

But housing prices in the US were a problem long before 2020 — and while demand is a big part of the story, there’s an even bigger reason it’s increasingly difficult for Americans to find affordable housing: We don’t have enough houses. According to one estimate, the US is now facing a nearly four-million-home shortage. And the primary reason for that shortage is what’s called exclusionary zoning.

Zoning laws are the local rules and regulations that decide what types of homes can be built where. These rules can sometimes have good intentions. But they also have a dark history in the United States as a tool to keep certain races, religions, and nationalities out of white neighborhoods. And while zoning laws in the US are no longer explicitly racist, their effect remains basically the same: to keep affordable housing, and the people who need it, away from the wealthiest Americans.

Today, in the majority of the US, especially in cities with good jobs, it’s illegal to build many affordable types of housing. And it’s led to a widespread affordability crisis. Watch the video above for more.

Sources:

Jerusalem Demsas reports on housing policy for Vox, and she’s written a ton about this issue:

Houses are getting more and more expensive. There’s a simple fix for that: https://www.vox.com/22464801/housing-bubble-market-crash-supply-shortage-great-recession

What it’ll take to fix America’s housing rules: https://www.vox.com/22252625/america-racist-housing-rules-how-to-fix

The housing shortage is making discrimination a lot easier: https://www.vox.com/2021/5/26/22453293/housing-supply-shortage-discrimination-real-estate-cover-letters

Why the housing market boomed despite the recession: https://www.vox.com/22264268/covid-19-housing-insecurity-housing-prices-mortgage-rates-pandemic-zoning-supply-demand

The zoning maps in the video came from UC Berkeley’s Othering & Belonging Institute: https://belonging.berkeley.edu/single-family-zoning-san-francisco-bay-area

Transcript
The national housing crisis

0:01 · So I spend a lot of time looking at houses on Zillow.

0:05 · And lately, I noticed that, even in places where houses are usually expensive…

0:10 · they seem even more expensive.

0:15 · Like here, in the San Francisco Bay Area.

0:19 · What has the last year been like?

0:34 · For years, the Bay Area has been an extreme example of how difficult it is to find affordable housing in the US.

0:41 · It’s where Silicon Valley bus drivers sleep in their cars at night, because they can’t afford housing near work.

0:48 · And where school teachers can’t afford to live in the counties they teach.

0:53 · But it’s not just the Bay Area.

0:55 · The lack of affordable housing is a national problem.

0:59 · And right now, it’s worse than ever.

1:02 · We’ve seen, over the last year, housing prices reach a level they’ve never reached before in American history.

1:08 · They kind of just look like a rocket ship going to the moon: housing prices reaching a median of $350,000 for the median American home.

1:16 · Those prices have made rents more expensive, and have made homeownership less attainable for millions of Americans.

Supply and demand imbalances

1:25 · So why is this happening?

1:27 · And how do we bring that rocket ship closer to Earth?

1:33 · We can think of today’s housing prices in terms of a supply-and-demand problem.

1:38 · On the demand side, there are a few things happening.

1:41 · The first is a generational shift in who’s buying homes.

1:45 · Millennials are the biggest generation in American history, and they’re aging into their prime home-buying years.

1:51 · On top of that, mortgage rates are at an all-time low, which means it’s very cheap to borrow the money needed to buy a house.

1:58 · That’s enticed more people to buy if they can, making demand for houses even higher.

2:04 · The problem is that supply isn’t matching that demand.

2:10 · From 2010 to 2019, there were fewer homes built in the US than in any decade since the 1960s.

2:18 · In particular, the construction of smaller, entry-level housing, the kind made for first-time home buyers, has dropped dramatically.

2:25 · In the 1980s, those “starter” homes made up around 40% of all homes built.

2:30 · Today, it’s closer to 7%.

2:33 · In 2018, one estimate said the US housing market was 2.5 million homes short of meeting demand.

2:41 · By the end of 2020, it was 3.8 million.

2:44 · And that’s driving a big part of the problem, both for renters and for people who want to be homeowners.

2:49 · The shortage is worst in the places where demand is highest, near good jobs, transit, and schools.

2:55 · And one pretty straightforward solution to that is to just build more homes in those places.

Impact of zoning regulations

3:02 · But for years, there’s been one big obstacle to that: we aren’t allowed to.

3:08 · Take a look at this map of the Bay Area.

3:11 · It’s showing something called zoning, or local regulations that decide what can be built where.

3:16 · This much of the region is zoned for residential housing.

3:20 · In blue are areas zoned to allow multi-family housing, while the areas shaded in pink are zoned for single-family housing only.

3:30 · That’s 82 percent of all residential land in the Bay Area.

3:35 · What it means is that you’ve banned the ability for anyone to build anything other than a single unit of housing on that lot of land.

3:43 · And in many towns, like Atherton, they’ve excluded all multi-family housing from their neighborhoods.

3:50 · And that doesn’t just mean a giant apartment building.

3:52 · It means things like duplexes, things like fourplexes…

3:56 · Things like that are illegal in the majority of the country.

3:59 · This is an example of something called “exclusionary zoning.”

4:03 · It’s a big part of the reason for the housing supply shortage in the US.

4:07 · And single-family-only zoning is just one way local laws limit how much housing we can build.

4:13 · Many places also employ height restrictions.

4:16 · In Cupertino, California, some areas are zoned for multi-family buildings, but they don’t allow any buildings over two stories.

Zoning barriers and segregation

4:27 · Parking requirements are often written into zoning laws, too.

4:30 · Cupertino requires developers to set aside space for two parking spaces for each unit of multi-family housing.

4:37 · That means, if you were building an apartment complex that had 100 units, you’d need to find space for 200 parking spots.

4:45 · Which usually means buildings that size don’t get built at all.

4:49 · They lower the number of units they’re actually building so they can save space for those parking spaces.

4:55 · And then, those units become more expensive because the land still stays the same cost to the developer.

5:00 · And you then get a situation where potentially more affordable units turn into higher-income-servicing units.

5:09 · Another feature of many zoning laws is minimum lot sizes.

5:12 · It means builders are legally required to allot a minimum amount of land for each home.

5:18 · Often a large amount of land.

5:21 · In Cupertino, most single-family lots must be at least 5,000 square feet each.

5:26 · Starter homes are usually around 1,400 to 1,500 square feet.

5:31 · And so you’ve basically banned all that type of housing.

5:34 · In Atherton, the minimum lot size for homes is one acre: more than 43,000 square feet.

5:41 · Which makes it virtually impossible to build any kind of affordable home there.

5:46 · Together, exclusionary zoning laws like this push builders across the country to focus on bigger, luxury homes, instead of smaller starter homes, or multi-family housing.

5:57 · Essentially creating gated communities in public spaces.

6:00 · What you are saying is that you are only allowing people who have already been able to partake in the wealth of this country, and to grow their income, and have access to high opportunity jobs and education, to live in our neighborhoods.

6:11 · Historically, some of the first zoning laws in the US were engineered for that exactly: to block people of color, and in particular Black Americans, from living in predominantly white neighborhoods.

6:22 · Today, the laws don’t explicitly mention race, but they continue to worsen segregation.

6:28 · In the Bay Area, the more single-family zoning in a neighborhood, the whiter it is.

6:34 · But all this has another effect as well: By shrinking the pot of new housing getting built, while demand keeps rising, it drives up the cost of housing for everyone.

Resistance to local changes

6:46 · Changing zoning laws can be difficult.

6:49 · And often, the biggest obstacles are the wealthiest residents.

6:52 · The process is usually defined by who shows up to these public meetings.

6:56 · And what you have is often a much whiter, wealthier crowd, the ones who come and say, “I don’t want this in my community,” “I’m concerned about what will happen to my property values.”

7:05 · And then there’s this kind of code word, “neighborhood character.”

7:09 · Remember those teachers I mentioned, who can’t afford to live in the counties where they teach?

7:14 · Well in 2018, one local school district proposed a solution: building affordable housing units for teachers in San Jose.

7:22 · It caused an uproar among San Jose parents, who petitioned against “changing the neighborhood.”

7:28 · It may not seem like a big deal when one wealthy neighborhood blocks one multi-family development.

7:34 · The problem is that it happens all the time: Communities block new housing everywhere.

7:39 · People are, when they hear this kind of rhetoric, very confused.

7:42 · Because they’re like, “I don’t want to live in a place with ten thousand apartment buildings.

7:47 · It doesn’t make sense to do that.”

7:49 · And they’re right. No one is saying that every neighborhood in every city should be ten thousand-foot apartment buildings or anything like that.

7:58 · But even small, gradual changes to zoning laws can have an impact.

8:02 · For example, allowing smaller homes on smaller lots, or simply allowing duplexes, would double capacity for housing in some areas.

8:12 · In recent years, some cities like Berkeley, Minneapolis, and Portland have taken the huge step of ending single-family zoning.

8:20 · But the problem is nationwide.

Statewide and federal solutions

8:22 · The real fix is going to happen when these decisions start being made, and start being regulated, at the statewide level or at the federal level in some capacity.

8:31 · Today, the Biden administration is attempting to tackle exclusionary zoning through a five billion-dollar program, that would give money to localities that remove exclusionary zoning policies.

8:41 · But even that may not be enough.

8:44 · This is more than any presidential administration has done on this topic, either Democrat or Republican.

8:51 · It is also very small in the face of this problem.

8:54 · They want to take action, they recognize how big of a deal it is, but they are not actually willing to create the kind of political blowback from often very high-value voters living in suburban environments.

9:06 · Ending America’s housing shortage will require real political willpower.

9:11 · And it’ll require people across the country to take a look at their own neighborhoods: what gets built, who gets excluded, and how to make homeownership achievable for the millions who are shut out.
